questions.q: What best describes an AI evasion attack?
options: Poisoning the training data so the model learns wrong patterns
Stealing the model's weights and parameters
Crafting inputs at inference time to make a trained model produce a wrong output, without changing the model
Overloading the model with too many requests until it crashes
questions.explanation: Evasion attacks trick an already-trained model at the moment it makes a decision. The model itself is never changed, only the input it receives is crafted to slip past it.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a training-time attack and an evasion (inference-time) attack?
options: Training-time attacks change what the model learned; evasion attacks only change the current input
Evasion attacks require access to the training pipeline; training-time attacks do not
There is no meaningful difference between the two
Training-time attacks only work on image models
questions.explanation: Training-time attacks corrupt the model's memory, affecting all future predictions. Evasion attacks leave the model untouched and only manipulate the specific input being evaluated right now.

questions.q: What does 'transferability' mean in the context of evasion attacks?
options: The ability to move a model from one server to another
An attack built against one model often fools a different model too, even a black-box one the attacker never inspected
The process of retraining a model on new data
Transferring stolen data to an external server
questions.explanation: Transferability lets attackers prepare and test their attack on a surrogate model they control, then successfully use that same attack against a real, unseen black-box system.

questions.q: Why is the Naive Bayes 'independence assumption' a weakness the GoodWords attack exploits?
options: It makes the model too slow to respond in time
It causes the model to reject any unusual word combination outright
It encrypts the word probabilities so attackers cannot read them
It treats each word's evidence separately and additively, so unrelated appended words simply shift the total without penalty
questions.explanation: Because Naive Bayes sums up evidence from each word independently, appending enough 'good' words can mathematically outweigh the spam signal, regardless of whether the words make contextual sense together.

questions.q: For a classifier with a decision boundary at 0.5, which statement is TRUE about successful evasion?
options: The attacker must drive the spam probability all the way to 0.01
Crossing the 0.5 threshold is enough; a score of 0.499 evades just as well as 0.01
The attacker must change the model's threshold to below 0.5
Evasion is impossible unless the model is retrained
questions.explanation: Classification is a binary decision at the threshold. Once the score crosses to the other side of 0.5, the label flips, so there's no benefit to pushing the score further than necessary.

questions.q: In a black-box GoodWords attack, what does the 40-40-20 budget allocation refer to?
options: 40% ham words, 40% spam words, 20% neutral words
40 queries per word, 40 words per message, 20 messages per test
40% accuracy, 40% recall, 20% precision
40% exploration, 40% exploitation, 20% combination search
questions.explanation: This is a proven split for allocating a limited query budget: 40% discovering new candidate words, 40% refining the best ones found, and 20% hunting for synergistic word combinations.

questions.q: In the multi-armed bandit framing of a black-box GoodWords attack, what does 'pulling the lever' correspond to?
options: Restarting the target server
Testing a candidate word by adding it to a message and querying the classifier
Changing the classifier's decision threshold
Downloading the model's source code
questions.explanation: Each candidate word is treated like a slot machine with an unknown payout. Testing it, by adding it to a message and querying the model, is the equivalent of pulling that machine's lever.

questions.q: What is the purpose of epsilon in an epsilon-greedy word selection strategy?
options: It sets the maximum message length allowed
It controls the probability of exploring a new word instead of exploiting the best-known word
It determines how many queries the API allows per second
It encrypts the query traffic
questions.explanation: Epsilon is the small probability, such as 0.2, of choosing to explore an untested word rather than exploiting the current best-performing word, balancing discovery against reliability.

questions.q: Why does measuring a single word's impact typically cost two queries rather than one?
options: One query for the baseline message and one for the message with the word added, so the difference reveals the word's true impact
APIs always require duplicate requests for verification
One query is for training and one is for testing
The classifier randomly fails half the time
questions.explanation: You need a baseline probability and an augmented probability to calculate the actual reward of adding a word, which is why a 1000-query budget yields roughly 500 word measurements, not 1000.

questions.q: What is 'synergy' in the context of combining words during a GoodWords attack?
options: When two words together produce a larger effect than simply adding their individual effects would predict
When a word works on one classifier but not another
When the attacker uses two different query budgets simultaneously
When a word is tested twice for reliability
questions.explanation: Synergy occurs when a combination like 'meeting tomorrow' scores much better together than the sum of 'meeting' alone plus 'tomorrow' alone would suggest, since together they read as more genuinely coherent language.

questions.q: Roughly how effective is a black-box GoodWords attack compared to a white-box attack against the same target?
options: About 10-20% as effective
Roughly equal, at 100% effectiveness
Roughly 85-95% of white-box effectiveness
Black-box attacks are always more effective than white-box
questions.explanation: Even without access to the model's internals, a patient black-box attacker using query-based discovery typically achieves 85-95% of what a white-box attacker with full model access could achieve.

questions.q: Why can the GoodWords technique be generalized from spam filters to sentiment classifiers?
options: Sentiment classifiers use a completely different mathematical approach
The technique works against any additive text classifier that reads bag-of-words, regardless of what labels it predicts
Sentiment classifiers cannot be attacked at all
Sentiment analysis requires physical access to the server
questions.explanation: Since GoodWords exploits the additive, order-blind nature of certain classifiers rather than anything spam-specific, the same technique applies to sentiment models or any other bag-of-words classifier.

questions.q: In sentiment flipping, what would an attacker append to push a negative review toward a positive classification?
options: Random punctuation marks
Strongly negative-leaning words
Strongly positive-leaning words, such as 'excellent' or 'wonderful'
The same review text repeated twice
questions.explanation: To flip a negative review to positive, the attacker appends words strongly associated with the positive class, which pushes the overall additive score across the decision boundary.

questions.q: Which defense most directly breaks the assumption that GoodWords relies on?
options: Increasing the server's rate limit
Returning only the label and hiding the probability score
Storing the model in an encrypted file
Adding n-gram (word-pair) features so context is considered, not just isolated word counts
questions.explanation: N-gram features consider word pairs like 'free money' together, breaking the independence assumption that lets isolated good words simply outvote suspicious phrases in an additive model.

questions.q: What does 'feature capping' do as a defense against GoodWords-style attacks?
options: It deletes all features associated with negative words
It limits how much a single word can shift the overall classification score, reducing the payoff of piling on words
It caps the number of users allowed to query the model
It encrypts individual word features
questions.explanation: By limiting the maximum influence any single word can have on the final score, feature capping reduces the effectiveness of an attacker simply appending many good words to overwhelm the classifier.

questions.q: According to the module, why is hiding a model's internals (obscurity) considered a weak defense on its own?
options: Obscurity makes models run slower
A determined black-box attacker can empirically rediscover the same winning words through repeated querying
Hiding internals is illegal under most security frameworks
Obscurity only works against white-box attacks
questions.explanation: The vulnerability lives in the model's architecture itself, not in exposed parameters. A query-only attacker can still discover effective words through trial and error, achieving most of white-box effectiveness.

questions.q: In the module's VULN / HARD / GUARD defense modes, what is the primary purpose of GUARD mode?
options: To make the model completely immune to all evasion attempts
To emphasize detection and monitoring, catching attacks in progress even when they can't be fully blocked
To disable the classifier entirely for safety
To encrypt all incoming messages before classification
questions.explanation: GUARD mode focuses on visibility rather than prevention: logging query patterns, rate anomalies, and message drift so that an in-progress attack can be noticed and escalated to a SIEM.

questions.q: Why does the module recommend testing both white-box and black-box evasion during a real assessment?
options: Because white-box testing is illegal in most jurisdictions
Because black-box access reflects how most real attackers actually interact with deployed systems, while white-box reveals the theoretical worst case
Because clients always insist on both tests
Because white-box and black-box use completely unrelated techniques
questions.explanation: White-box testing is faster and shows the worst-case scenario, but real attackers rarely have model access, so confirming the attack also works black-box reflects genuine, realistic risk.

questions.q: Why should a penetration tester report the full effectiveness curve (evasion rate vs. words added) rather than a single evasion number?
options: A single number is always more accurate than a curve
The curve reveals exactly where the filter's defenses collapse, which a single number would hide
Curves are required by law in security reports
It makes the report longer and therefore more credible
questions.explanation: Reporting only one evasion percentage hides useful detail. The full curve shows the client precisely how many words it takes before their filter fails, which is far more actionable information.

questions.q: Which industry framework is specifically referenced in the module as the adversarial-ML knowledge base under which evasion attacks are categorized?
options: MITRE ATLAS
PCI DSS
HIPAA
questions.explanation: MITRE ATLAS is the adversarial machine learning threat knowledge base, where evasion attacks fall under categories like ML Model Access and Evade ML Model techniques.
